hook.text: Every model in a dbt project runs as a query in a warehouse, and the warehouse sends a bill.

hook-bill.text: What the bill counts depends on the warehouse: the bytes a query scans, or the time its compute runs.

plan.text: Ten questions get worked through, and three come quickly at the end. No vendor's warehouse runs here. Sizes are measured in DuckDB, an analytics database, on a million sales made up for this video, and anything bigger is a model, said as one.

split.text: Question one. What makes a modern cloud warehouse different from a traditional one?

split-new.text: Storage is separate from compute. Snowflake, BigQuery and Databricks, three cloud data platforms, keep the data in cheap object storage and start compute that reads it. So you scale query power without moving data, and run many isolated workloads over one copy.

split-old.text: A traditional warehouse, like an on-premises Teradata or classic Redshift, couples the two: they grow together, whether you need both or not.

split-catch.text: The catch: compute you can start, you can also leave running, and where compute is billed by the second, it bills the whole time.

arch.text: Question two. How do Snowflake, BigQuery, and Redshift differ architecturally?

arch-snow.text: Snowflake keeps storage apart from compute clusters you define, called virtual warehouses, and manages its micro-partitions itself.

arch-bq.text: BigQuery is serverless: no clusters to size. You pay per byte scanned, or for reserved slots, and it partitions and clusters the tables you declare.

arch-rs.text: Redshift is cluster-based: provisioned nodes, with distribution and sort keys you choose, though Redshift Serverless and RA3 nodes have moved it toward separate storage.

oltp.text: Question three. What is the difference between OLTP and OLAP systems?
oltp.spoken: Question three. What is the difference between OLTP and oh-lap systems?

oltp-def.text: OLTP, online transaction processing, serves many small reads and writes of single rows, with strict consistency: an app's Postgres, stored by row. OLAP, online analytical processing, serves a few large scans and aggregations: the warehouse, stored by column.
oltp-def.spoken: OLTP, online transaction processing, serves many small reads and writes of single rows, with strict consistency: an app's Postgres, stored by row. Oh-lap, online analytical processing, serves a few large scans and aggregations: the warehouse, stored by column.

oltp-flow.text: So data is extracted from the first, loaded into the second, and transformed there. That last step is the analytics engineer's.

oltp-heavy.text: Run heavy analytics on the app's own database instead, and it competes with the app, and runs badly.

cols.text: Question four. What is columnar storage, and why does it matter for analytics?

cols-def.text: It keeps each column's values together on disk, instead of each row's. An analytical query touches a few columns across many rows, so it reads only those columns.

cols-compress.text: And values of one type, side by side, compress far better. A million region names take five and a half megabytes as text, and three hundred eighty kilobytes as one encoded column.

cols-rows.text: Row stores still win at reading whole rows one at a time. Column stores win at aggregating billions of them.

star.text: Question five. Why does select star cost more in a columnar warehouse?

star-model.text: Because the scan follows the columns you name. The page's model: on a two hundred column table, three columns are one and a half percent of the data, if every column is the same width. Select star is all of it, and on per-byte billing you pay for every byte.

star-run.text: Measured in DuckDB, on the million sales: select star read the whole nine point four megabyte file. Units by region, two columns, read under eight hundred kilobytes.

star-wide.text: It's bytes, not column count. Amount, random to the cent, is nearly half the file, so revenue by region read four point six megabytes.

star-dbt.text: In a project, name the columns: a model built as a table from select star reads every column of its source on every build.

prune.text: Question six. What is partitioning, and how does partition pruning save money?

prune-def.text: Partitioning splits a table into segments by a column, usually a date. A query that filters on that column reads only the matching segments, and skips the rest. That's pruning.

prune-model.text: The page's model: a year of data at two point four gigabytes a day. Unpartitioned, every query reads all eight hundred seventy-six gigabytes. Partitioned by day, a seven-day dashboard tile reads sixteen point eight: about fifty times less, and billed that way.

prune-run.text: In DuckDB, with the million sales in a folder per month, a query for March scans one file of twelve. Filter on region instead, and it reads all twelve: pruning only works on the partition column.

prune-not.text: And a query over all of history saves nothing, which is why the answer isn't to partition everything.

cluster.text: Question seven. What is clustering, and how does it differ from partitioning?

cluster-def.text: Clustering sorts rows inside storage, so the engine can skip blocks that can't match a filter. In the sales file, each block of rows records its first and last date. In date order, March overlaps two blocks of nine. Shuffled, every block spans the year, and the same query read five times the bytes.

cluster-diff.text: Partitions are coarse, a few large segments, often with a cap on how many. Clustering is fine-grained, and handles columns with many values.

cluster-rule.text: So partition by date, and cluster by the high-cardinality keys your filters use.

hurt.text: Question eight. When can partitioning or clustering hurt more than help?

hurt-small.text: When the partitions are tiny. Split the million sales by day, and you get three hundred sixty-six files of about twenty-seven kilobytes. Their footers alone come to two hundred six kilobytes, against under five for one file, and reading the year opens every file.

hurt-cluster.text: And clustering on a column no query filters buys nothing, while the sorting still costs maintenance.

hurt-rule.text: Partition and cluster on the columns filters actually use, and match the grain to the volume: a million rows a year is too few to split by day.

compute.text: Question nine. What is a virtual warehouse, or slot, or compute cluster, and how does it drive cost?

compute-def.text: It's the compute that runs the queries, sized apart from the storage. Snowflake bills credits per second while a warehouse runs. BigQuery bills the bytes scanned, on demand, or reserved slots. Redshift bills its provisioned nodes.

compute-model.text: Here's a model, not a measurement. Say a dashboard keeps a cluster busy for two minutes an hour. Billed by time and left running, you pay for sixty minutes.

compute-lever.text: That's why the billing model matters: it tells you which lever cuts the bill, less data scanned or less compute time.

obt.text: Question ten. Why is a wide, denormalized one big table sometimes preferred in a warehouse, and when is it appropriate?

obt-def.text: It pre-joins the dimensions into the fact: one flat table, every attribute a column. Queries skip the joins, and dashboard tools that struggle with many tables get just one.

obt-cheap.text: Columnar storage makes the copies cheap. On the million sales, the category name on every row compresses to three hundred eighty kilobytes, the same as the integer key it replaces.

obt-cost.text: The cost is maintenance. Rename one category, and the star updates one row. The wide table updates almost two hundred thousand, in every block of the file.

obt-where.text: So serve a wide table at the end, where speed matters, and keep the star upstream as the source it's rebuilt from.

r-cost.text: Question eleven. How do you control warehouse cost in practice? Scan less: prune, name columns, store expensive repeated logic as tables rather than views, and build big append-only tables incrementally. Compute less: right-size, suspend when idle, and keep ad hoc queries off the production warehouse, so they can't starve the pipelines.

r-cache.text: Question twelve. What is a result cache, and how does it help? It returns a stored result for the exact same query over unchanged data: instantly, and often for free. So it rewards queries that don't vary, and any change to an underlying table invalidates it.

r-dist.text: Question thirteen. What are distribution and sort keys in Redshift? A distribution key decides which node holds each row: distribute on the join key, and matching rows meet without a shuffle across the network. A sort key orders rows on disk, so range filters skip blocks. Pick a key one value dominates, and one node does most of the work: skew.

next.text: Every lever here makes a model cheaper. None of them makes it right, and a cheap model that's wrong costs more than any scan. Next: testing and data quality.

compute-bytes.text: Billed by bytes on demand, idle time costs nothing, and only the scan counts.

star-limit.text: And on BigQuery, a limit doesn't help: it bills the columns scanned, not the rows returned.

hurt-month.text: Even by month, each file is tiny. At this size, don't partition at all.

compute-suspend.text: Suspended when idle, about two, plus the wait before each suspend, so keep that wait short.
